newsitem.title: USA: CBOT, farm groups square off over delivery changes.
newsitem.headline: CBOT, farm groups square off over delivery changes.

text.p: The architect of the Chicago Board of Trade's controversial plan to change delivery terms of its soybean and corn contracts defended the proposal on Wednesday before skeptical leaders of nearly two dozen U.S. farm groups and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission

Craig Pirrong, a professor at Washington University in St. Louis and a member of the CBOT's delivery task force, said the decision to drop Toledo as a delivery point for the two big contracts was essential despite opposition from Ohio's congressional delegation, scores of agricultural groups and big grain traders such as Cargill and Louis Dreyfuss.
The proposed change reflects the greater market clout of the nation's western corn belt, he said. More U.S. production and processing plants are located in the western corn belt.
"A single delivery point is easily understood and helps in arbitrage and spread trading," Pirrong told the CFTC's agricultural advisory committee.

Members of the committee include the American Farm Bureau Federation, the American Soybean Association, the National Corn Growers Association and a dozen other influential farm groups. Most expressed skepticism about the CBOT plan at the meeting.
The CBOT proposal, now awaiting CFTC action, would drop Toledo and St. Louis in favor of ports along the northern Illinois River.

The exchange put forward the plan only after the CFTC pressed the CBOT last December for a change because of concern about market manipulation from rapidly-disappearing grain warehouses in Chicago. But farmers and politicians have insisted that Toledo remain as a delivery point to serve the interests of the eastern corn belt.

Paul Architzel, the CFTC chief counsel, said the agency had the power to force the exchange to modify its proposal. "If we find they (the CBOT delivery changes) are not appropriate we have authority under appropriate procedures to require that the contract be supplemented or amended," Architzel said.

Pirrong rejected a possible compromise put forward by the CFTC in a letter last week in which the agency urged CBOT to modify its proposal by keeping Toledo along with the new northern Illinois River delivery ports.
"Changes to the proposal could upset the delicate balance overall," Pirrong said. Keeping Toledo would mean a "one to two percent hedging decline in effectiveness" in the contracts.

"Do I give the two percent hedging difference to 80 percent of the market in the western corn belt, or give it to 20 percent of the market in the eastern corn belt?" Pirrong added. "That's the fundamental issue here."
And Steve Patton, representing the National Council of Farmer Co-ops, urged the CFTC "to give this matter more study" before deciding on the CBOT proposal.

"We're rushing headlong into something that's untried and unproven," said Patton, who also is an executive with Indian's CountryMark Cooperative Inc, one of the firms likely to lose business if Toledo was dropped as a delivery point.
The CBOT delivery proposal is one of the most contentious issues to come before the agency, which has been deluged with more than 370 letters and faxes, mostly opposing the plan.

The battle between the agency and the world's largest futures exchange escalated last week when the CFTC told CBOT it had illegally listed certain soybean and corn contracts for trading in 1999 without agency approval. The contracts were the first to include the new terms that eliminated Toledo.
